/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.headline: Is London really the most-taxed city? Banks accused of cherrypicking data
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.excerpt: A banking lobby group has been accused of cherrypicking data and trying to mislead the British government by claiming a tax rise for banks at next week’s budget would leave London less competitive than rival financial hubs. UK Finance, which represents banks including Lloyds, JP Morgan and Revolut, commissions an annual report tallying up all the taxes shouldered by a large bank, including corporation tax, social security, VAT and bank-specific levies. The report, put together by PwC, lists London as the most tax-intensive city, charging a “total tax rate” of 46.2%, compared with 42.2% in Amsterdam, 39.1% in Frankfurt, 29% in Dublin and 27.9% in New York. The figures have been heavily pushed by UK Finance, including in a recent letter to John Healey, the chancellor, in which it warned that banks could shift business and jobs to rival hubs if threatened with higher bills. However, questions are now being raised about the lobby group’s data. They include why Paris, one of London’s biggest rival financial hubs and host to many large investment banks including JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs and Barclays, has consistently been excluded from UK Finance comparisons. Calculations by the Guardian, which were reviewed by a leading accountancy firm, show that the same bank in Paris would face a total tax rate of between 51.6% and 57.3%. That is up to 11.1 percentage points higher than London.
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.trail: Lobby group’s figures, shared with John Healey, are misleading as they do not include major rival Paris, say campaigners

/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.headline: John Healey pledges to use budget to harness power of AI to bolster Britain’s security
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.excerpt: John Healey has pledged to use Wednesday’s budget to harness the power of artificial intelligence to bolster Britain’s security and prosperity against the risks in the accelerating global technology arms race. As he prepares for his debut budget, the chancellor said that Andy Burnham’s government would commit hundreds of millions of pounds to develop a “distinctively British” approach to AI that would capitalise on the benefits of the frontier technology. At a fork in the road as AI developments pose both existential threats and transformative economic potential, Healey said he would be making the biggest ever investment to guard against cyber risks and the disruptive potential of the technology. As part of the measures in his tax and spending statement, he promised fresh investment for Britain’s AI Security Institute and other critical institutions, alongside allocating public money to support the use of the technology for good. “AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school and every aspect of our economy can benefit,” Healey said.

/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.headline: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advances
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.excerpt: Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-saving plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI. The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year. The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, told reporters on Thursday that the job cuts were part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. “These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5,000 full-time employees. Around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive.” When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to advances in AI, the chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes. “That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said, calling AI the “icing on the cake” to modernising the bank’s technology. Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said Barclays workers “deserve better”. She added: “The company is using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce. Employers should be focused on upgrading employees’ skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace.

In an interview for a Guardian series looking at how Britain can reverse the declining fortunes of towns, the former Bank of England chief economist urged them to launch a realignment of the tax system away from favouring online sellers, alongside a review of business rates and measures to turbocharge devolution. “The balance of tax incentives are strongly skewed towards the digital over the physical, and the large over small, and if you’re serious about high streets that needs somehow rebalancing,” he said. Calling on Burnham to follow through with Labour’s manifesto promise to “replace” the business rates system, Haldane said “some levelling of the playing field” was needed to help smaller operators who faced soaring costs and evaporating demand. “One of the reasons why high streets are dying, and some of the towns, is business rates are punitive for smaller shops,” he said. “This needs to be wrapped up with that more fundamental review of business rates and I’ll hope we see that in the budget.

/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.headline: Double blow to Healey as inflation rises to 3.5% and monthly deficit hits £24bn
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.excerpt: Inflation surged to 3.5% last month while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn, in a double dose of bad news for John Healey before next week’s budget. The Office for National Statistics said annual inflation rose from 3.1% in August, overshooting City forecasts of a rise in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 3.4%, as a result of the surging cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have soared since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, throttling the flow of fuel through the strait of Hormuz. Rising inflation has also contributed to higher government borrowing costs – the key factor behind the deterioration in the public finances since the spring statement in March. Official figures showed the government paid £10.9bn in debt interest last month: the highest September figure since records began, and only the eighth time the monthly number has been above £10bn. Payments on some government bonds rise in line with inflation. The ONS said higher inflation had added £4bn to debt interest costs in September alone. Total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time – although as a share of the size of the economy it has fallen to 94%, from 95% a year ago. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £97.8bn, the ONS said – £4.4bn lower than last year, but still £6bn higher than the independent Office for Budget Responsibility had expected.
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/andy-burnham-john-h.trail: Consumer prices rise by more than expected while government’s debt interest payments surge to record high for September

/world/2026/oct/25/myanmar-aung-san-suu-.headline: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles
/world/2026/oct/25/myanmar-aung-san-suu-.excerpt: Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s King Charles to Aung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation. A presidential spokesperson said on social media that home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment. Photos showed the Nobel Peace laureate smiling in a wood-panelled room, a paper calendar on the wall behind her. Suu Kyi, 81, the daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San, has spent much of her life in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. She is now serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw, the capital. Over her lifetime, the country’s military rulers have been cautious about locking Suu Kyi away in prison due to her beloved domestic status and international prominence, particularly in Britain, where she lived and married an Oxford academic. Most other political prisoners languish in jail. Despite winning a 2015 election, she was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the independent conflict monitor ACLED.

/world/2026/oct/25/myanmar-aung-san-suu-.excerpt: Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi has met a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the aid organisation has confirmed. The meeting on Monday ⁠followed years of questions over the wellbeing of the 81-year-old, whose whereabouts and health condition have been largely unknown since the elected civilian government she led was ousted by a military coup in February 2021. Little has been seen or heard of Aung San Suu Kyi since late 2022. Myanmar’s military-backed administrations have repeatedly claimed she is in “good health”, even as international pressure has grown on the country’s government to allow independent verification. Aung San Suu Kyi’s son, Kim Aris, who had recently demanded the ruling junta provide proof of life, welcomed news of the meeting. He described it as “the first positive development concerning her in more than five years”, adding: “This is an important first step, but it must not be the last,.” In a social media post, Aris said he hoped the meeting would lead to “greater humanitarian access, direct contact with my mother, credible and independently verified information about her wellbeing, and ultimately her immediate and unconditional release, together with all political prisoners”. On Monday, Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative of the ICRC to Myanmar, visited Aung San Suu Kyi in the capital, Naypyidaw, the government spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said in a post on Telegram.

/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.headline: EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence
/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.excerpt: EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027. EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine, but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will call on the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, to contribute to Ukraine’s looming financial shortfall at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week. A similar request to the British prime minister will be made when he meets von der Leyen and the European Council president, António Costa, for a long-awaited EU-UK summit on 20 November in Brussels. It comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, prepares for his first budget next week, weighing numerous calls for more spending against the rising cost of government borrowing and a darkening economic outlook. Healey said earlier this month he was “working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine – military, diplomatic and economic”. Ukraine says it faces a €70bn (£58bn) funding shortfall in 2027 to pay for its defence and civilian needs. The EU and its member states are paying for 80% of Ukraine’s financial needs, according to the commission, which considers a “fair” EU share to be two-thirds, with the remaining third covered by other allies.

/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.headline: Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.excerpt: In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said. “This is a decision that lasts for life.” Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify. A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe. This week he went further, insisting the current arrangement must change: “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.” Among a range of options on the table, he has been clear, is the possibility of going “all the way” and rejoining the EU. There are pressing economic reasons Burnham has been talking up closer alignment, as the EU works out its position on the UK’s access to its protectionist “Made in Europe” legislation, which the prime minister has said could hurt British manufacturing. But after years of bitter division and political dysfunction in the fallout from the vote, are the British public really ready to talk about Brexit again – and even to contemplate reversing it? Polling evidence may suggest so.
/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.trail: As Andy Burnham talks up closer alignment with the EU and a poll suggests half in UK would rejoin, the B-word is back on the agenda

/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.headline: Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.excerpt: Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said. Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”. He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU. The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU. It is mainly aimed at China, which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland. “It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry. “We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added. Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.

/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.headline: Russia did try to interfere in Brexit referendum, head of MI5 confirms
/politics/2026/oct/25/andy-burnham-says-.excerpt: Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum through social media and television reports, the head of MI5 said on Tuesday, but he added that did not mean the Kremlin had any impact on the result. Ken McCallum endorsed comments by Andy Burnham, who raised the issue over the past two days, though he said continuing to debate it risked giving the Kremlin a needless propaganda victory. During an annual threat update, the head of Britain’s domestic intelligence agency said the Russian-owned English-language broadcasters RT and Sputnik “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” with biased anti-migration and anti-EU reports. He said there had also been “a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”: an unspecified number of fake social media accounts, operating largely on X, that had sought to influence the result. Neither tactic was particularly sophisticated or successful, the spy chief said. There was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”. Both interference attempts have been previously cited in studies released in the years after the Brexit vote. The digital campaign group 89up said RT and Sputnik had published 261 mostly misleading articles highlighting immigration and other anti-EU issues that achieved 134m potential page impressions.

/world/2026/oct/24/hundreds-of-thousands.headline: Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases
/world/2026/oct/24/hundreds-of-thousands.excerpt: Awa, 18, stood in the dock in the tribunal de Paris, a small, mute and bewildered figure seeming unable to understand, let alone answer, the simplest of questions. The court was told she had joined young people who looted an Yves Saint Laurent store on Boulevard Saint Germain in Paris’s Left Bank late on Sunday and stripped it bare within minutes. Awa was arrested at a nearby Métro station with a black balaclava and black gloves in her backpack along with four YSL handbags worth a total of €5,000 (£4,200). In the dock, dressed entirely in black – the clothes she was wearing when arrested two days earlier – she appeared panicked, clutched at her hair, picked her lip. Unable to speak, she covered her face and began to weep; first silently, then uncontrollably, her sobs punctuating an almost palpably painful silence. Awa was just one of 2,500 people arrested during last weekend’s rioting and looting across the country, more than 900 of whom are being fast-tracked through the courts using a procedure called comparution immédiate (immediate appearance). It sends them to trial straight or shortly after being taken into custody, or within three days if they are held in pretrial detention. The process of handling this sudden influx of cases has overwhelmed the courts and angered defendants’ lawyers, who say they have no time to meet clients. The violence erupted after high-school student and union demonstrations.
/world/2026/oct/24/hundreds-of-thousands.trail: Politicians have called for ruthless sentencing, but lawyers blame the politicians for the poverty, and anger, behind their clients’ looting

Speaking over clips of fires in France, with the chyron “A warning from Europe” emblazoned on the screen, Hannity said: “This is, sadly I argue, by design – an attempt by the left to destroy the free world, western civilisation, if you will.” He added: “This is a preview of coming attractions here in America.” Hannity wasn’t alone. On Monday, Fox News host Laura Ingraham had on Jamie Metzl, who describes himself as a “technology and healthcare futurist [and] geopolitical expert”, to draw the same comparison. “If you like what you’re seeing in France then you should support these DSA candidates who are essentially calling for the same thing here,” Metzl said. He was only echoing something Ingraham herself had said a few days earlier, in front of a cartoon version of a police flashing light with the words “A warning to America”. The chyron, as she spoke, could not have had a clearer message.

/world/2026/oct/24/hundreds-of-thousands.headline: French borrowing costs overtake US amid budget turmoil
/world/2026/oct/24/hundreds-of-thousands.excerpt: French borrowing costs continued to rise on Thursday, as investors fret that France’s government is struggling to pass a federal budget after public protests gripped the country. France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 years. The yield on the French 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat) – rose by nine basis points to 5.089% in early trading on Thursday, its highest level since July 2022. It broke across the 5% threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The move lifted France’s 10-year borrowing costs over the equivalent for US Treasury bonds for the first time since 2013. The volatility comes as the French government struggles to pass a budget for next year, while the country recovers from widespread protests that turned violent last weekend. Tens of thousands of people had attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille in recent days. Public buildings were attacked, and thousands of shops and businesses were looted. The interior ministry said there had been nearly 2,400 arrests.

Asked if he was referring to Donald Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” The US president has blamed France’s violence on “migrants, jihadists and communists” as he campaigns for his Republican party before midterm elections. Macron told reporters in Doha that some leaders “in the middle of election campaigns, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic” were “naively spreading narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote”. They were “using our country for their own political campaigns”, the French president said. “And we don’t need that. We already have difficulties to deal with.” He said AI-generated images were circulating “depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.” The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections next weekend, has also said that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”.

In Germany – where there were no major protests – the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has stoked fears rioting could spill over the border. /uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.headline: Barriers facing black and south Asian music events ‘cost London up to £141m a year’
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.excerpt: Black and south Asian music events in London face disproportionate cancellations, restrictions and licensing barriers compared with white events, according to a two-year investigation into racial inequality in the capital’s live music industry. The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing (REMEL) report, led by Black Lives in Music, estimates that cancellations, displacement and events prevented from taking place cost London £127m to £141m annually, with projected losses exceeding £650m over five years. The report found that genres including Afrobeats, drill and dancehall are routinely labelled “high risk” despite a lack of credible evidence, while indie, pop and rock events face comparatively little scrutiny. Other events facing stringent restrictions included reggae gatherings aimed at older audiences, jazz nights and community events. The research raised concerns over the use of unverified police intelligence, with promoters describing events being cancelled based on undisclosed information, online searches or unrelated incidents. Charisse Beaumont, chief executive of Black Lives in Music, said that although the investigation focused on London, the problems it uncovered exist nationwide. “As soon as we put the report out there, the call for our survey, people were upset that they couldn’t complete the survey because they were outside of London,” she said. For Beaumont, the discrimination extended far beyond specific music genres. “It’s about race.
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.trail: Exclusive: Investigation finds racial inequality in live music industry rife and many genres labelled ‘high risk’ despite lack of evidence

/uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.headline: Met chief says ‘toxicity’ around DEI will not stop him recruiting more black and Asian officers
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.excerpt: Mark Rowley has said the Metropolitan police must recruit more black and Asian officers in order to gain the trust of minority ethnic communities in London, and vowed not to be “blown off course by the culture wars”. The right has criticised drives for diversity, claiming they lead to lower standards. Rowley, who is commissioner of the Met and Britain’s top police officer, said that as a leader of a major organisation he was prepared to take a stand against the “toxicity” surrounding the diversity debate and criticised other leaders for “running away from the subject”. In London, 46% of people are from a minority ethnic background, compared with 18% of Met officers. Rowley said he was driven by operational necessity, not politics, and believed “inclusivity” was vital to policing by consent, which is the philosophical cornerstone of British policing. “We cannot police London effectively if we fail to recruit from all of London,” he writes in the Guardian. “Effective policing depends upon inclusivity. If you are committed to policing by consent which stands or falls on the trust of all communities, you cannot do without it.” He writes: “Today, we are launching a major recruitment campaign. We have no interest in the politics and ideologies of the culture wars. Inclusion is an operational necessity. “We cannot be effective if large sections of society do not trust us, do not work with us or do not see policing as a service that understands their experiences.
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.trail: Sir Mark Rowley says inclusivity is crucial for the force and he refuses to be ‘blown off course’ by critics

/uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.headline: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.excerpt: Tom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts. Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer. Palantir was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and has provided AI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is under significant pressure from Labour MPs and unions to ditch Palantir from government contracts, including a £330m software deal with the NHS. The company is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. It is seeking to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annual turnover of £427m. Watson told the BBC podcast Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: “One of the things I’d say to my former colleagues is: do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?
/uk-news/2026/oct/24/manhunt-under-way-t.trail: Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns

/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.headline: ‘We can’t let the far right take power again’: Lula voters in final push before Brazil runoff
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.excerpt: Naiara Boroni, Nikolas Domingues and Jodersson Diego live in the same city and do not know one another, but said they had done the same thing in recent days: persuaded at least one person who had not voted for the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round to choose him in this Sunday’s runoff. In Boroni’s case, it was her grandmother who had not turned out; in Domingues’s, a cousin who had chosen a candidate who finished fourth. But Diego achieved what to many sounds almost impossible in such a polarised country: he said he had persuaded a woman who voted for the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro to switch sides. “She’s a student of mine and didn’t vote for Lula because of her evangelical church. I didn’t argue; I tried to explain that he wasn’t everything they said he was, and she said she had changed her mind,” said Diego, 33, a dance teacher from Belo Horizonte, the capital of the state of Minas Gerais. Winning over voters who abstained or cast null votes, and flipping as many others as possible, is at the heart of Lula’s strategy as he tries to do what no presidential candidate has ever managed in Brazil: overturn a first-round defeat like the one he suffered to Bolsonaro on 5 October. Lula received 3.8 million fewer votes than in 2022, when he ran against the senator’s father, then president Jair Bolsonaro – who would go on to lose the runoff and try to stage a coup, which failed after the heads of two of the three armed forces refused to join him.
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.trail: In bellwether Minais Gerais, with polls about even, president’s supporters are striving to win over those who abstained or voted for Flavio Bolsonaro

/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.headline: ‘This is a lethal threat’: Indigenous groups fear Bolsonaro’s hold on voters in Brazil’s Amazon towns
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.excerpt: It was the night before the first round of Brazil’s presidential election and Rosimari Monteiro was so excited she couldn’t sleep. The 38-year-old spent hours tossing and turning at her home in the Amazon town of Mucajaí before rising at dawn to cast her vote. “I was the first person to vote at my polling station … I voted 22, so we got off to a positive start,” recalls Monteiro, as she stands in her sitting room with her two young daughters. Twenty-two is the number Brazil’s electronic voting system uses to identify the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who is hoping to beat the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in this year’s election. “To us, he represents the future. We want a light at the end of the tunnel. We want a better future for ourselves and for our kids, who are the future of our nation,” enthuses Monteiro, who was far from the only person in Mucajaí to vote Bolsonaro. In fact, this sun-baked roadside settlement is where Bolsonaro secured his biggest proportional victory in Roraima, the northern state where the would-be president also registered his best nationwide result. Nearly 79% of 11,734 votes in Mucajaí went to Bolsonaro. Monteiro gave several reasons for her decision, including Bolsonaro’s pledges to fight crime and create jobs. But one issue explains why the son of the disgraced former president Jair Bolsonaro is so popular here and across Roraima, where 14 of 15 municipalities backed the far-right politician.
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.trail: Far-right presidential candidate is popular among those who believe more mining can help revitalise local economies

/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.headline: Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoff
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.excerpt: Five days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could. Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour. Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign. Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”. The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro just days before next Sunday’s runoff and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”. Late last week, justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze said he had found no evidence of deliberate action by the company, which would require further investigation, but he gave Meta 24 hours to prove that the problems affecting Lula had been fixed and would not happen again.
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.trail: Lula’s supporters suspect tech firm meddling on behalf of US president Donald Trump, who has close ties to Bolsonaro family

/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.headline: ‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.excerpt: Earlier this month, Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva led a rally in São Paulo, as he aims to be re-elected to a fourth presidential term, and faces serious opposition from right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro. Taking the mic before a crowd on Avenida Paulista that organisers put at more than a million, the former union leader began: “I’m not sure whether to open this speech with ‘comrades’ or ‘fandoms from all over Brazil’.” The rally was organised by Lula’s Workers’ party (PT) and a string of other leftwing groups – but the spark came from pop music fandoms. More than 600 Brazilian fanbase groups for Billie Eilish, Lady Gaga, Katseye, Demi Lovato, Harry Styles, Katy Perry, Selena Gomez, as well as Brazilian stars such as Anitta, Marina Sena and Ludmilla among others, all came together to back Lula, waging an intense online campaign as soon as Lula’s rival, son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, came out on top in the first round on 4 October. Neither candidate earned more than 50% of the vote, so a runoff is now scheduled for 25 October to decide between the two. When the first round results came in, “I had this feeling I’d seen it all before with Jair Bolsonaro, and that was really frustrating,” says V, a Billie Eilish fan who helps run Info Billie Brasil, one of the country’s biggest fan communities dedicated to the US singer.
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.trail: Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their mission

/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.headline: The ‘Finger cutter’ and the ‘Brazilian Escobar’: the men accused of bringing cocaine cartels to Europe
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.excerpt: In the early hours of 7 September, a convoy of heavily armed police swept through the sleeping streets of central Brussels towards the Haren district, on the city’s north-eastern outskirts. They made their way to 22 Avenue du Bourget, a militarised bunker-like complex that was the former headquarters of Nato. The modernist complex, with its austere and functional architecture, was hastily built in 1967 and houses the Justitia courtroom, where Belgium’s federal trials are now held. It was here that the perpetrators and accomplices of the 2015 Paris terrorist attacks and the 2016 Brussels attacks were tried in 2022. Last month, officers armed with assault rifles patrolled the building’s wide corridors, protecting those involved in this decade’s most high-profile trial: the Bressers-Carvalho case. For a month, judges and a legion of lawyers shared the main courtroom with journalists and the public on one side of a large armoured-glass partition. On the other side were the defendants, 31 in number, flanked by officers with their faces masked to protect them from possible reprisals. It was a scene more typical of countries ravaged by mafias. During the lengthy hearings throughout the month, two among the many defendants stood out. The first was Flor Bressers, a 40-year-old Belgian born in Lommel, a town of 35,000 in the province of Limburg. Bressers has an unusual profile for criminal circles.
/world/2026/oct/24/lula-da-silva-support.trail: A Belgian criminal organisation’s links with a Brazilian cocaine gang have been the focus of a major trial in Brussels, where smuggling links have been alleged between European players and the drug cartels of Latin America
